drop.title: When a Coin's Worth Leaves Its Seat

title: When a Coin's Worth
Leaves Its Seat
slides.dek: Turning Turtles said a heads coin is worth its position. Change the move a little and the worth becomes the ruler sequence, then the odious numbers, and yet the same XOR still names the winner.

slides.body: A row of coins, each heads or tails. Turn one heads coin down, maybe flip some coins to its left, and whoever turns the last head down wins. Read the heads as a binary number and every legal move makes it strictly smaller, so the game must end, which is enough for one theorem to name the winner: a board is worth the *XOR* of its heads' worths, and you win by driving that XOR to zero. That machine never changes. The only knob is *which coins you may flip along with the one you turn down*, and turning it quietly changes what a single coin is worth.

In *Turning Turtles* a heads coin at position k is worth exactly k, the seat it sits in. Give the move more reach, flip the whole run up to the coin, and in *Ruler* its worth becomes the largest power of two dividing k: 1, 2, 1, 4, 1, 2, 1, 8, the tick heights on a ruler, so every coin on an odd seat is worth just 1. Allow *two* extra flips and you get *Mock Turtles*, where a coin is worth the k-th odious number, 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, the integers with an odd count of 1-bits, the Thue-Morse parity. Four heads worth 1, 2, 4 and 7 already XOR to zero: you have lost, and nothing on the board looks lost.

three games over one engine, switchable at the top: a playable board vs a machine that enumerates its legal moves and plays perfectly by construction, a value ladder drawing each game's g(k), and the XOR reasoning table shared by all three

checked offline with a full minimax, no XOR assumed: the three closed forms match the single-coin values for k=1..12; g(board) = XOR of head worths over every board to width 9, 0 mismatches / 1536; every winning board to width 10 has a move to XOR 0; every mock turtles value is odious

slides.big:
one machine,
three prices for
*the very same coin.*
slides.sub: Play all three games against a machine that never errs: Turning Turtles, where a coin is worth its seat; Ruler, where it is worth the largest power of two dividing its position; and Mock Turtles, where it is worth the odious numbers, the Thue-Morse parity. Same board, same XOR reasoning table, three completely different value ladders. Turn a head down to remove its worth from the XOR, and use the flips to its left to make every binary column even again.
